New Jersey Adopts First-in-Nation Rules Requiring Operators to Flag At-Risk Gamblers

Published October 27, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

New Jersey has adopted new, legally binding rules requiring online casino and sports wagering operators to proactively identify at-risk customers, state officials announced in late October. Officials describe the regulations as the first mandatory, data-driven responsible gambling standards of their kind in the country — moving the state beyond voluntary best practices and self-exclusion lists toward enforceable detection requirements.

What the new rules require

Under the regulations, every licensed operator must designate a responsible gaming lead and apply mandatory thresholds tied to gambling activity and behavioral indicators to flag customers who may be at risk. Once a customer meets those criteria, the operator must conduct a due-diligence review of that player's account history and, if warranted, add them to an at-risk patron list. From there, operators must carry out a three-phase intervention process calibrated to the customer's assessed level of need — a structured escalation rather than the one-size-fits-all warning messages or static deposit-limit tools many platforms have relied on previously.

Officials' comments

Gov. Mikie Sherrill said the state "continues to lead the way in developing data driven best practices for Internet gaming and online sports wagering." Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said the state is "proud to enact regulations that require operators to offer resources, including live support if appropriate, to those struggling with problem gambling." State officials said similar responsible gambling practices existed at individual operators before this, but not under a uniform standard that carries the force of law.

Why it matters

New Jersey is one of the largest regulated online gambling markets in the country, and its rules have a track record of influencing how other states approach iGaming oversight. The move follows the state's Division of Gaming Enforcement launching RecoverMe, a free app offering cognitive-behavioral and mindfulness-based support tools, as its second free problem-gambling resource after the GamFin financial-counseling service introduced last year. The new detection requirements add a proactive, operator-side obligation on top of those player-facing resources, at a time when federal lawmakers have separately been pressing several sportsbooks over how their VIP programs identify and market to heavy losing customers.
